text: Education begins with stories, since children hear stories before they train their bodies (Republic II, 376e–377a). The founders of the city must supervise the makers of stories, and Socrates lays down two laws governing what may be said about the gods. The first is simple: God is good, and because God is good, God is the cause only of good things. The evils in the world far outnumber the goods, so some cause other than God must be found for them, since nothing good can cause harm (379b–380c). The second law is that God does not change and does not deceive. Whatever is in the best condition is least altered by outside forces, and a perfect being would never willingly change for the worse (380d–381c). Homer's story of the two jars at Zeus's threshold must be excluded, as must poets who blame a god for the ruin of a household and stories of gods who change their shape. The lie that gods and human beings hate most is the lie in the soul, not the spoken lie: being deceived about reality in the most important part of oneself (382a–382c). A god has no such lie in the soul, and no motive to put one in anyone else's soul.
